content: Many individuals with epilepsy experience poorly controlled seizures despite the availability of current antiepileptic treatments. Due to the high prevalence of treatment resistance, there is growing interest in exploring new pharmacological options, such as pregabalin. However, the robustness of existing evidence supporting the use of pregabalin as monotherapy remains uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of pregabalin in individuals with epilepsy. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Epilepsy Group's Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Chinese Biomedical Literature Database, covering studies up to August 2012. No language restrictions were applied during the search. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared pregabalin with either a placebo or another antiepileptic drug used as monotherapy for epilepsy. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the quality of the included trials. The outcomes evaluated included: (1) time to withdrawal after randomization, (2) time to achieve six-, 12-, or 24-month remission, (3) the proportion of participants who remained seizure-free for six or more continuous months, (4) time to first seizure after randomization, (5) validated quality of life measures, (6) health economic outcomes, and (7) adverse effects. Time-to-event outcomes were expressed as hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), where an HR > 1 indicated that the event was more likely to occur earlier with pregabalin than with the comparator. Two short-term studies involving a total of 753 participants met the inclusion criteria. One study compared pregabalin with lamotrigine in patients with newly diagnosed partial seizures, while the other compared pregabalin with gabapentin in hospitalized patients with refractory partial epilepsy. No studies were identified that addressed generalized-onset tonic-clonic seizures, either alone or in combination with other generalized seizure types. When compared to lamotrigine, pregabalin demonstrated inferior outcomes in several key measures. Specifically, pregabalin was associated with a higher likelihood of withdrawal due to inadequate seizure control after dose stabilization (HR 4.52; 95% CI 1.93 to 10.60). Pregabalin also showed a lower likelihood of achieving six-month remission after dose stabilization (HR 0.56; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.76) and a reduced proportion of participants who remained seizure-free for six or more continuous months (RR 0.76; 95% CI 0.67 to 0.87). Regional differences were observed, with the clinical disadvantage of pregabalin being more pronounced in Asia (RR 0.70; 95% CI 0.57 to 0.86) compared to Europe (RR 0.83; 95% CI 0.69 to 0.99) and the Americas (RR 0.62; 95% CI 0.33 to 1.19). Additionally, pregabalin was associated with a shorter time to first seizure after dose stabilization (HR 1.74; 95% CI 1.26 to 2.39). While there were no significant differences in safety-related outcomes between pregabalin and lamotrigine, participants in the pregabalin group were more likely to experience somnolence, weight gain, and convulsions. In comparison to gabapentin, pregabalin demonstrated better outcomes in terms of time to withdrawal for all reasons after randomization (HR 0.25; 95% CI 0.11 to 0.57) and time to withdrawal due to inadequate seizure control (HR 0.41; 95% CI 0.18 to 0.92). However, no significant differences were observed in safety-related outcomes between the two drugs. It is important to note that limitations in the study design, such as short-term follow-up and low initial target dose selection, may have influenced the results. In conclusion, pregabalin appears to have similar tolerability but inferior efficacy compared to lamotrigine for newly diagnosed partial seizures. The observed regional differences, particularly the more pronounced clinical disadvantage of pregabalin in Asia, warrant further investigation into potential ethnic variations in treatment response. The data comparing pregabalin and gabapentin were too limited to draw definitive conclusions. Additionally, this review does not provide guidance on the use of pregabalin for patients with generalized-onset tonic-clonic seizures. Further long-term trials are necessary to establish the true effectiveness of pregabalin as monotherapy for epilepsy.
